title: 那是你的工位  (That Is Your Desk)

segments.t: After Bu Xiaogu jumps in backstage to help with a costume emergency, Wang Er leads her into Xingtian's open-plan production floor, explains the rival departments, and shows her to her desk right outside Chun Yuqiao's office. Listen first.
工资还没拿呢，就干上活了？
我看他们太忙了，就想上去帮把手。
今天是最轻松的一天了。
你真正的战场应该是在这边。
星天有很多部门，这些部门之间都是平行的。
最重要的部门还是这边，淳于乔领导的制作部。
那儿就是淳于乔的总编室。
那是你的工位，你坐那儿。
你们好，我叫布小谷！
Let's walk through what Wang Er tells her. First he teases Xiaogu for pitching in before she is even on the payroll.
工资还没拿呢，就干上活了？

'You have not even collected your pay yet, and you have already started working?' Pairing "hai mei", 'still have not', with "jiu", 'already', highlights how surprisingly fast the second thing happened, and "gongzi" means 'salary'.
我看他们太忙了，就想上去帮把手。

'I saw they were too busy, so I wanted to step up and lend a hand.' Colloquial "bangbashou" literally says 'help a hand' — the everyday spoken equivalent of lending a hand when colleagues look swamped.
今天是最轻松的一天了。
'Today is actually the easiest day.' Put "zui" before any description to form 'most', so "zui qingsong" means 'most relaxed' or 'easiest'.
你真正的战场应该是在这边。
'Your real battlefield should be over here.' Office veterans love calling the main desk floor a "zhanchang", literally 'battlefield', while "yinggai" expresses what ought to be the case.
星天有很多部门，这些部门之间都是平行的。

'Xingtian has many departments, and all of these departments are on equal footing.' Adding "zhijian" after a group means 'between' or 'among them', and "pingxing" literally means 'parallel', with neither side outranking the other.
最重要的部门还是这边，淳于乔领导的制作部。

'Still, the most important department is right here: the production unit led by Chun Yuqiao.' Notice "haishi" here: rather than asking 'or', in a statement it weighs options and concludes 'still, after all'.
那儿就是淳于乔的总编室。
'Over there is Chun Yuqiao's chief editor's office.' Adding "jiushi" instead of plain "shi" points right at a landmark — 'that right there is' — and "zongbianshi" is the chief producer's hub.
那是你的工位，你坐那儿。
'That is your desk — you sit over there.' Chinese offices call an individual workstation a "gongwei", literally 'work spot', and "zuo" means 'sit'.
你们好，我叫布小谷！

'Hello everyone, my name is Bu Xiaogu!' Greeting one person uses "ni hao", while greeting several deskmates at once switches to plural "nimen" in "nimen hao". Now let's listen to the whole office arrival scene again.
工资还没拿呢，就干上活了？
我看他们太忙了，就想上去帮把手。
今天是最轻松的一天了。
你真正的战场应该是在这边。
星天有很多部门，这些部门之间都是平行的。
最重要的部门还是这边，淳于乔领导的制作部。
那儿就是淳于乔的总编室。
那是你的工位，你坐那儿。
你们好，我叫布小谷！
Xiaogu has found her desk, even if her exhausted neighbours barely look up from their screens. You learned "gongwei" for a desk spot, "bangbashou" for lending a hand, and plural "nimen hao".
